Title: SQL Injection in get_user
Analysis:
### Source
The path parameter `{username}` from `/users/v1/{username}` is passed to `get_by_username()` in `api_views/users.py`, which calls `User.get_user(username)`.

### Sanitization/Validation
When the application is in vulnerable mode (`vuln = 1`), no sanitization, escaping, or parameterized query placeholders are used.

### Sink
The string is directly interpolated into a raw SQL query `SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}'` and executed via `db.session.execute(text(user_query))` on line 73.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A request with a SQL injection payload:
`GET /users/v1/name1' UNION SELECT 1,username,3,password FROM users LIMIT 1 -- HTTP/1.1`
This executes as:
`SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'name1' UNION SELECT 1,username,3,password FROM users LIMIT 1 --'`
and returns password data of another user or leaks details.
Snippet:
if vuln:  # SQLi Injection
            user_query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}'"
            query = db.session.execute(text(user_query))
            ret = query.fetchone()
            if ret:
                fin_query = '{\"username\": \"%s\", \"email\": \"%s\"}' % (ret[1], ret[3])
            else:
                fin_query = None

Title: BOLA / IDOR in Password Update
Analysis:
### Source
The path parameter `{username}` in `/users/v1/{username}/password` is supplied by the user.

### Sanitization/Validation
The token validator checks who owns the JWT (`resp['sub']`), but there is no validation checking if `resp['sub']` matches the path parameter `{username}` when `vuln` mode is enabled.

### Sink
On lines 187-190, the application queries the user by the path-provided `username` parameter and updates their password to `request_data.get('password')`, enabling arbitrary password resets.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
As an authenticated user `attacker`, send a request:
`PUT /users/v1/victim/password`
With Header:
`Authorization: Bearer <attacker_jwt>`
And body:
```json
{
  "password": "hacked_password"
}
```
This bypasses authentication but updates `victim`'s password instead of `attacker`'s.

Title: BOLA / IDOR in retrieving book by title
Analysis:
### Source
The path parameter `book_title` from `/books/v1/{book_title}` is supplied by the user.

### Sanitization/Validation
The token validator decodes the token, but in `vuln` mode (`vuln = 1`), there is no check ensuring that the currently logged-in user (`resp['sub']`) is the owner of the requested book.

### Sink
On line 51, the application queries the book by `book_title` without scoping the query to the authenticated user. This leaks the secret content of the book.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
As an authenticated user, request a book belonging to another user:
`GET /books/v1/some_other_users_secret_book`
With Header:
`Authorization: Bearer <user_jwt>`
This returns the book's details, including the `secret` field, which should only be visible to its owner.

Title: Mass Assignment / Privilege Escalation in Register User
Analysis:
### Source
The POST request body payload at `/users/v1/register` is supplied by the user.

### Sanitization/Validation
The JSON schema `register_user_schema` allows additional properties such as `admin` to be parsed without restriction.

### Sink
If `vuln` mode is enabled and `admin` is in `request_data`, the application sets the user's `admin` property directly to `True` if requested, leading to Privilege Escalation.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A registration POST request:
`POST /users/v1/register`
Body:
```json
{
  "username": "attacker",
  "password": "password123",
  "email": "attacker@example.com",
  "admin": true
}
```
This registers the new user with administrative privileges.

Title: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) in email validation
Analysis:
### Source
The request body parameter `email` from `PUT /users/v1/{username}/email` is supplied by the user.

### Sanitization/Validation
The application checks the email format with a regular expression containing overlapping/nested repetition groups:
`^([0-9a-zA-Z]([-.\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z])*@{1}([0-9a-zA-Z][-\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z]\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,9})$`

### Sink
When evaluated using Python's backtracking regex engine `re.search()`, an input with many nested repetitions can cause exponential backtracking, locking up the CPU/worker thread (Regular Expression Denial of Service - ReDoS).

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A request with a payload crafted to trigger exponential backtracking:
`PUT /users/v1/name1/email`
Body:
```json
{
  "email": "a" + "-"*50 + "!"
}
```
This causes the thread evaluating `re.search` to hang, leading to resource exhaustion.
Snippet:
if vuln:  # Regex DoS
            match = re.search(
                r\"^([0-9a-zA-Z]([-.\\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z])*@{1}([0-9a-zA-Z][-\\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z]\\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,9})$\",
                str(request_data.get('email')))
